name: Ultimate Attribution Error
description: In intergroup settings, people often give their own group more charitable causal stories than the out-group: bad acts by “them” look dispositional, while good acts by “them” get explained away as luck or exception. It is a specifically intergroup version of attribution bias, with prejudice embedded in the explanation pattern.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to moderation, marketplace disputes, cross-team conflict, support operations, and user-research synthesis. Teams can read out-group communities' failures as character while treating in-group failures as context or bad luck.
myth_risk_note: Hewstone's (1990) review across 19 studies explicitly reports 'only limited support' for Pettigrew's full ultimate-attribution-error formulation, despite finding narrower, consistent ingroup-serving attribution patterns on three specific dimensions (internal attribution for positive ingroup acts, ability-based explaining-away of outgroup success, and preference for ingroup-serving group-difference attributions). The broader 'ultimate attribution error' as a single unitary phenomenon is less robustly supported than its component sub-biases.
prevalence_note: A recognizable label in intergroup-attribution and prejudice research, but very rarely named explicitly in ordinary product-design practice outside specialized fairness or social-science-aware discussions.

findings.description: Across 19 studies of intergroup causal attribution, Hewstone found recurring ingroup-serving attribution patterns, but only limited support for Pettigrew's full "ultimate attribution error" as a sweeping general rule. The strongest evidence favored more internal explanations for ingroup positive acts, more dispositional explanations for outgroup failures, and a tendency to explain away outgroup success as luck, effort, or situational advantage.
findings.source_title: The ‘ultimate attribution error’? A review of the literature on intergroup causal attribution
